The Story of Knowledge-Giving

I bow to Lord Jina, who carries beings across the ocean of existence, and I write the story of knowledge-giving as the cause of attaining happiness.

I bow to that Bharati Saraswati, whose originator is Lord Jina, and who is the stick that destroys the veil of ignorance that blocks knowledge of objects from the eyes. Just as collyrium is applied with a stick to cure eye diseases, or a stick made of such substances that destroys all eye diseases, so too the Saraswati-Jinwani stick destroys the disease of ignorance. With its help, knowledge of objects comes very easily.

I bow to those monks who are conquerors of delusion, adorned with the three jewels — right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct — and whose lotus feet are the abode of all happiness, the Lakshmi.

Having thus worshipped God, guru, and scriptures, the story of the knowledge-giver is briefly written here so that upon reading it, the holy thought of knowledge-giving may awaken in the hearts of noble souls. Knowledge is the supreme eye of all living beings. One who does not have this eye, even though having physical eyes, is blind. His life has no value. Therefore, to make a worthless life valuable, one should certainly give the gift of knowledge. This is the king of all gifts. Other gifts will satisfy desires for a short time and one life only, but through knowledge-giving, the desires of birth after birth are destroyed, and both the giver and the receiver reach that infinite place where there is nothing but knowledge, where knowledge itself becomes their soul. This is the matter of the next world. Besides this, in this world too, through knowledge-giving, the giver's pure fame spreads in all directions. The entire world praises him with a hundred mouths. Such people receive their desired honour wherever they go. Therefore, knowledge-giving gives both enjoyment and liberation.

Therefore, worthy souls should, as their duty, themselves give knowledge-gifts and encourage others onto this pure path. One thing to note about this knowledge-gift is that it should be accompanied by rightness — meaning it should be such that no living being is harmed, that there is no opposition or fault in it.

This story teaches that knowledge-giving is the supreme form of charity. While other forms of giving satisfy temporary needs, knowledge-giving transforms the very soul of both giver and receiver. It leads not only to worldly success but ultimately to liberation. The wise should therefore dedicate themselves to spreading true knowledge, especially spiritual knowledge, for this is the greatest service one can render to the world.
